https://openalex.org/W3042981350.title: Molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease
https://openalex.org/W3042981350.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder seen in age-dependent dementia. There is currently no effective treatment for AD, which may be attributed in part to lack of a clear underlying mechanism. Studies within the last few decades provide growing evidence for a central role of amyloid β (Aβ) and tau, as well as glial contributions to various molecular and cellular pathways in AD pathogenesis. Herein, we review recent progress with respect to Aβ- and tau-associated mechanisms, and discuss glial dysfunction in AD with emphasis on neuronal and glial receptors that mediate Aβ-induced toxicity. We also discuss other critical factors that may affect AD pathogenesis, including genetics, aging, variables related to environment, lifestyle habits, and describe the potential role of apolipoprotein E (APOE), viral and bacterial infection, sleep, and microbiota. Although we have gained much towards understanding various aspects underlying this devastating neurodegenerative disorder, greater commitment towards research in molecular mechanism, diagnostics and treatment will be needed in future AD research.

https://openalex.org/W3044413849.title: Impaired glymphatic function and clearance of tau in an Alzheimer’s disease model
https://openalex.org/W3044413849.abstract: Abstract The glymphatic system, that is aquaporin 4 (AQP4) facilitated exchange of CSF with interstitial fluid (ISF), may provide a clearance pathway for protein species such as amyloid-β and tau, which accumulate in the brain in Alzheimer’s disease. Further, tau protein transference via the extracellular space, the compartment that is cleared by the glymphatic pathway, allows for its neuron-to-neuron propagation, and the regional progression of tauopathy in the disorder. The glymphatic system therefore represents an exciting new target for Alzheimer’s disease. Here we aim to understand the involvement of glymphatic CSF-ISF exchange in tau pathology. First, we demonstrate impaired CSF-ISF exchange and AQP4 polarization in a mouse model of tauopathy, suggesting that this clearance pathway may have the potential to exacerbate or even induce pathogenic accumulation of tau. Subsequently, we establish the central role of AQP4 in the glymphatic clearance of tau from the brain; showing marked impaired glymphatic CSF-ISF exchange and tau protein clearance using the novel AQP4 inhibitor, TGN-020. As such, we show that this system presents as a novel druggable target for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease, and possibly other neurodegenerative diseases alike.

https://openalex.org/W3145545686.title: Sleep deprivation impairs molecular clearance from the human brain
https://openalex.org/W3145545686.abstract: Abstract It remains an enigma why human beings spend one-third of their life asleep. Experimental data suggest that sleep is required for clearance of waste products from brain metabolism. This has, however, never been verified in humans. The primary aim of the present study was to examine in vivo whether one night of total sleep deprivation affects molecular clearance from the human brain. Secondarily, we examined whether clearance was affected by subsequent sleep. Multiphase MRI with standardized T1 sequences was performed up to 48 h after intrathecal administration of the contrast agent gadobutrol (0.5 ml of 1 mmol/ml), which served as a tracer molecule. Using FreeSurfer software, we quantified tracer enrichment within 85 brain regions as percentage change from baseline of normalized T1 signals. The cerebral tracer enrichment was compared between two cohorts of individuals; one cohort (n = 7) underwent total sleep deprivation from Day 1 to Day 2 (sleep deprivation group) while an age and gender-matched control group (n = 17; sleep group) was allowed free sleep from Day 1 to Day 2. From Day 2 to 3 all individuals were allowed free sleep. The tracer enriched the brains of the two groups similarly. Sleep deprivation was the sole intervention. One night of sleep deprivation impaired clearance of the tracer substance from most brain regions, including the cerebral cortex, white matter and limbic structures, as demonstrated on the morning of Day 2 after intervention (sleep deprivation/sleep). Moreover, the impaired cerebral clearance in the sleep deprivation group was not compensated by subsequent sleep from Day 2 to 3. The present results provide in vivo evidence that one night of total sleep deprivation impairs molecular clearance from the human brain, and that humans do not catch up on lost sleep.

literature.summary:
Executive abstract

Our synthesis identifies several converging themes in dementia prevention, intervention, and molecular pathogenesis that are shaping current research priorities. There is an emerging consensus that Alzheimer-type dementia arises from interacting molecular cascades—principally involving amyloid-β and tau—modulated by glial dysfunction, APOE genotype, aging biology, and diverse environmental and lifestyle factors. This multifactorial view reframes targets beyond single-pathway drug discovery toward approaches that integrate modulation of neuronal–glial signaling, host vulnerability (genetic and age-related), and upstream risk modification. A parallel theme is the growing emphasis on earlier, mechanism-informed diagnostics and multimodal prevention strategies across the life course rather than late-stage monotherapies.

Complementing molecular insights, a novel and rapidly developing strand of evidence implicates brain fluid dynamics and sleep in proteopathic clearance and disease propagation. Findings coalesce around the idea that aquaporin-4–dependent CSF–interstitial fluid exchange (glymphatic-like processes) contributes to removal of extracellular tau and other metabolites, that impairment of these clearance pathways can accelerate regional tau accumulation, and that even short-term sleep loss measurably reduces molecular clearance in humans. Together these themes suggest promising, complementary intervention avenues—improving sleep and sleep-dependent clearance, targeting fluid-transport mechanisms, and coupling these with molecular and glial-directed therapies—while underscoring the need for rigorous translational and longitudinal work to define causal pathways, therapeutic windows, and personalized prevention strategies.

critique.summary: The literature provides structural support for the first causal link: one night of total sleep deprivation can impair molecular/glymphatic clearance and is associated with increased peripheral (and possibly CSF) tau biomarkers in humans. However, the subsequent steps of the chain—regionally specific (limbic) stagnation that measurably increases extracellular tau dwell time/concentration, rapid conformational conversion to seeding‑competent oligomers, short‑term increases in neuron‑to‑neuron tau transfer, and cumulative propagation from repeated acute episodes—are not directly demonstrated in the cited evidence. The current body of work supplies plausible proximal mechanism (impaired clearance) but lacks direct, regionally resolved, temporally precise, and mechanistic measurements that would connect impaired clearance after a single night to increased local seeding activity and accelerated network propagation.

full_output.structural_assessment: Partial alignment: the evidence aligns with the hypothesis for the initial impairment-of-clearance link (sleep deprivation -> reduced molecular/glymphatic clearance and elevated peripheral/CSF tau signals). Beyond that, the chain is speculative relative to the cited literature: no direct, region-specific measures of extracellular tau dwell time, no reported demonstrations of rapid conversion to seeding‑competent oligomers after one night, and no direct observation of increased short‑term neuron-to-neuron tau transfer or cumulative seeding burden from repeated acute episodes.
limitations: Human studies use surrogate tracers and peripheral/CSF biomarkers that do not directly measure extracellular ISF tau concentration or dwell time in specific brain regions (e.g., limbic nodes).
Small sample sizes and short follow-up in human tracer/biomarker studies reduce robustness and generalizability.

Temporal resolution is limited: demonstrations of impaired clearance after one night do not establish whether a single subsequent sleep episode fully restores clearance or whether impairment persists.
No direct evidence in the cited literature that acute sleep deprivation triggers conformational conversion of soluble tau to seeding‑competent oligomers in vivo.
Neuron‑to‑neuron transfer after single-night deprivation is not measured; transference studies typically require different experimental paradigms (animal models, labeled tau, biosensor assays).
Regional specificity (limbic-predominant stagnation) is asserted but not directly shown with regionally resolved tracer/ISF tau measurements in humans.

Potential confounders—acute stress, inflammation, circadian disruption, blood–brain barrier changes, or altered peripheral clearance—are not excluded and could account for increased peripheral tau signals.
Species differences limit extrapolation from animal glymphatic or tau-propagation data to human single-night effects (if such animal data exist but are not cited).
suggestions: Refine the hypothesis to separate: (A) acute impairment of glymphatic/ISF clearance and short-term biomarker changes, from (B) the downstream molecular events (dwell time, conformational conversion, transference) that require distinct, regionally resolved evidence and possibly a temporal accumulation threshold.

Prioritize experiments that directly measure extracellular ISF tau concentration and dwell time in limbic regions following one night of total sleep deprivation: e.g., in vivo microdialysis in animal models or CSF sampling combined with regionally targeted imaging in humans when feasible.

Evaluate seeding activity directly using tau biosensor amplification assays (RT-QuIC, cell-based tau seeding biosensors) on regionally sampled ISF/CSF after acute sleep deprivation to test conversion to seeding‑competent species.

Test short‑term neuron‑to‑neuron transfer empirically using labeled tau species and synaptically connected circuit models (organotypic slices or in vivo tracers) with and without acute sleep deprivation, and assess whether a single episode changes transfer probability.

Implement repeated-acute paradigms (serial nights of deprivation separated by recovery sleep) in animals to test cumulative effects on seeding burden and propagation, with longitudinal imaging/biochemical endpoints.

Control for confounders (stress hormones, systemic inflammation, BBB permeability, circadian phase) to distinguish glymphatic-specific effects from other mechanisms increasing extracellular tau or peripheral tau signals.

In human studies, increase sample sizes, include regionally informative imaging modalities (dynamic contrast/CSF tracers, diffusion MRI proxies of perivascular flow), and obtain CSF sampling timed to sleep/wake episodes to probe restoration after recovery sleep.

Specify operational definitions in the hypothesis (e.g., what magnitude/duration of impaired clearance constitutes 'not corrected by the next sleep episode', and what level of extracellular tau increase would be sufficient to promote seeding).

exploration_trace:
I followed the required exploratory strategy and used the graph tools repeatedly to build a causal picture connecting acute sleep loss to processes central to Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Below I (1) briefly state what I queried, (2) summarize the key graph-derived observations, (3) present plausible causal chains that tie them together (the “mechanistic hypotheses”), and (4) give targeted experiments and interventions that would test the most novel, non‑obvious predictions.

What I queried (tool log, high level)
- Started by retrieving central nodes to orient myself.
- Inspected neighbors for: “One night of total sleep deprivation”, “glymphatic system”, “Impaired cerebral clearance”, “tau protein transference”, “CSF‑ISF exchange”, “Cerebral tracer enrichment”, “Subsequent sleep”, and “Alzheimer’s disease (AD)”.
- Ran path searches linking sleep deprivation → tau transference and sleep deprivation → AD and also explored glymphatic → tau and impaired clearance → tau.

Key graph observations (facts from the KG)
- “One night of total sleep deprivation” is linked to impaired molecular/cerebral clearance observed across most of 85 quantified brain regions (cerebral cortex, white matter, limbic structures). The impaired clearance on the morning after sleep loss was not compensated by subsequent sleep.
- The glymphatic system (AQP4‑facilitated CSF–ISF exchange) provides a clearance pathway for both amyloid‑β and tau; it clears extracellular space and interstitial fluid.
- Tau spreads via extracellular space enabling neuron‑to‑neuron propagation and regional progression of tauopathy.
- AD node connects to tau and amyloid‑β, and to glial dysfunction, APOE, aging, lifestyle — sleep is noted as a potential contributor to AD pathogenesis.
- Cerebral tracer enrichment and a 48‑h imaging window were used to quantify impaired clearance across 85 brain regions (i.e., measurable, regional effects).

Mechanistic, causal chains (novel, testable hypotheses suggested by connecting nodes)
1) Acute glymphatic impairment → extracellular accumulation → tau seeding and propagation
- One night of total sleep deprivation → impaired CSF–ISF/glymphatic clearance across many brain regions (especially limbic structures) → transient increase in extracellular soluble tau and amyloid‑β in affected regions → increased probability of tau protein transference via the extracellular space → neuron‑to‑neuron propagation and regional spread of tauopathy → over repeated episodes, accrual of pathology accelerates AD progression.
Novelty: the graph emphasizes that a single night produces measurable, regionally distributed impairment that is not corrected by the next sleep episode. That non‑compensation creates a possible “seeding window” after an acute sleep loss where extracellular tau encounters conditions favoring transference and establishment of propagation chains.

2) Regional vulnerability + network propagation hypothesis
- Sleep deprivation non‑uniformly impairs clearance (limbic structures and some white matter/ cortex regions are highlighted). Limbic regions are early sites of tauopathy; impaired clearance specifically in these nodes could increase local seeding likelihood. Because tau propagation follows neural connectivity, focal seeding in limbic nodes during repeated sleep loss would preferentially route tau through vulnerable AD networks.
Novelty: the idea that acute sleep loss repeatedly targets the same network nodes (limbic nodes) and thus biases initial seeding locations and propagation trajectories for tau pathology.

3) Glial/AQP4 modulation as an amplifier
- Glymphatic CSF–ISF exchange is AQP4‑facilitated. The graph also links glial dysfunction to AD. Acute sleep deprivation might alter astrocyte AQP4 polarization/function (or microglial clearance roles) -> reduce glymphatic flux and also change extracellular milieu (inflammation, proteostasis) that favors tau aggregation and transference.
Novelty: combining acute astrocyte/AQP4 dysfunction after sleep loss with regional glymphatic failure to provide a two‑hit mechanism that both raises extracellular tau and increases its transmissibility.

4) White matter clearance impairment as a conduit for propagation
- The graph shows white matter clearance impairment after one night of sleep loss. Impaired clearance in white matter pathways may slow interstitial fluid flow along axonal tracts, increasing dwell time of extracellular tau in periaxonal/perivascular spaces—thereby facilitating transfer along connected pathways.
Novelty: conceptualizing white matter clearance deficits not only as reduced removal but as a facilitator of path propagation along tracts.

Why these are non‑obvious and potentially high‑impact
- Prior models often treat chronic sleep disruption as a risk factor through cumulative amyloid or inflammatory effects. The KG suggests a single night causes measurable, regional, and non‑compensated clearance deficits — implying acute sleep loss could create discrete windows where seeding/transmission is particularly likely. That shifts emphasis from only chronic exposure to the importance of acute episodes and their timing relative to other insults.
- The regional specificity (limbic focus) and white‑matter involvement provide a mechanism for why tau (which propagates along networks) could preferentially originate/spread after sleep disruption.
- Highlighting AQP4/astrocyte dysfunction as an immediate amplifier links glial biology and extracellular transmission.

Direct, testable predictions / experiments
1) Human/clinical imaging and biomarker tests (short-term)
- After controlled one‑night total sleep deprivation in healthy volunteers: collect CSF/ISF (if possible) or blood/neurochemical biomarkers at morning and 24–48 h later; expect transient increases in soluble tau (and possibly oligomeric tau species) and reduced tracer clearance on glymphatic imaging; compare limbic vs non‑limbic regional tracer retention.
- Use dynamic tracer MRI (48‑h window as in dataset) to map regional enrichment; hypothesis: limbic and connected network nodes show disproportionate tracer retention after single-night sleep loss.

2) Animal mechanistic tests (causal)
- In awake rodents, perform single‑night sleep deprivation and quantify ISF tau levels, astrocyte AQP4 polarization, and microglial activation in limbic regions. Expect increased ISF tau and disrupted AQP4 polarization.
- Seed reporter tau in limbic nodes immediately before vs after sleep deprivation to test if sleep loss increases likelihood of successful seeding and faster propagation along connected pathways.
- Blockade/rescue experiments: inhibit AQP4 (e.g., TGN‑020 — noted in neighbors as impairing CSF–ISF exchange) to mimic sleep loss; conversely, enhance perivascular flow (pharmacologically or by increasing slow‑wave sleep) to test rescue of seeding probability.

3) Longitudinal cumulative model
- Expose animals to repeated single‑night losses (with normal recovery sleep) and measure whether repeated, non‑compensated clearance events lead to accelerated tau spread vs animals with continuous mild disruption or controls.

Potential interventions implied by the chain
- Preventing acute glymphatic failure after sleep loss (e.g., pharmacologic enhancers of AQP4 function/polarization or interventions that promote slow‑wave sleep immediately following enforced wakefulness) might reduce the chance of tau seeding/transmission.
- Targeted protection of limbic glymphatic flow (positioning, vascular interventions) after known acute sleep loss episodes (e.g., shift workers, medical residents) could be explored.

Limitations / what the graph does not yet show (gaps to fill)
- The KG shows associations (sleep loss → impaired clearance; glymphatic → tau clearance/transference), but direct, causal demonstration that human single‑night sleep loss increases extracellular tau transference and long‑term AD risk remains to be proven.
- Mechanistic link to AQP4/glial polarization is plausible from the nodes but not explicitly documented in the KG for single‑night sleep loss; this is a critical experiment to do next.

Summary (one‑sentence crisp take)
- The KG supports a novel, testable hypothesis that even a single night of total sleep deprivation produces regional glymphatic/CSF–ISF clearance failure (not compensated by subsequent sleep), creating transient extracellular accumulation and conditions that promote tau transference in limbic and connected networks — a mechanism that could seed and accelerate AD‑relevant tau propagation, amplified by astrocyte/AQP4 and white‑matter clearance dysfunction.

If you want, I can:
- Draft an experimental protocol (human or rodent) to test the most critical causal link (sleep deprivation → extracellular tau increase → increased seeding/transmission).
- Produce a prioritized list of biomarkers and imaging endpoints to maximize signal detection in a small clinical study.
structural_hole_analysis:
structural_hole_analysis:
Short answer: Yes — there is a plausible, testable bridge. The missing links center on clearance of interstitial/CSF solutes (the glymphatic/perivascular system, BBB/vascular transport) and how APOE, glial/neuronal receptor biology, Aβ and tau pathology modulate that clearance. Gadobutrol intrathecal/CSF tracer dynamics and delayed (≈48 h) cerebral enrichment provide an imaging window into that clearance; FreeSurfer can quantify regional retention. Together these can connect molecular Alzheimer’s biology (Cluster A) to tracer-based MRI phenotypes (Cluster B).

1) Structural holes (what’s missing between the clusters)
- No explicit mapping from molecular players (APOE isoforms, Aβ, tau, astrocyte/microglial receptors such as AQP4, LRP1, TREM2, LDLR family, etc.) to in vivo tracer-clearance metrics (gadobutrol enrichment at 48 h).
- Lack of longitudinal/cross-modal studies that: stratify tracer retention by genotype (APOE), by amyloid/tau PET status, and by measures of glial/vascular receptor function or localization.
- Limited mechanistic linkage between BBB/transcytosis pathways (LRP1-mediated Aβ transport, endothelial dysfunction) and delayed parenchymal tracer accumulation.
- Few standardized analytic pipelines (e.g., FreeSurfer ROIs + tracer maps) that tie regional tracer retention to regional vulnerability to Aβ/tau deposition and to receptor expression patterns.
- Missing animal↔human translational experiments that manipulate specific molecular nodes (AQP4 localization, ApoE isoforms, LRP1 expression) and measure tracer kinetics analogous to human 48-h gadobutrol MRI.

2) Plausible underlying mechanism? — Yes
Mechanistic concept: APOE genotype and receptor-mediated glial/endothelial functions determine efficiency of perivascular/CSF–interstitial fluid (ISF) exchange and transvascular clearance. Impaired clearance increases retention of interstitial solutes including Aβ and tau and also of extracellular MRI tracers (gadobutrol), so delayed cerebral tracer enrichment (measured at ~48 h) becomes a readout of impaired clearance. Mechanistic players: astrocytic AQP4 polarization/perivascular endfeet, endothelial LRP1 and other receptors mediating Aβ efflux, microglial receptors modulating phagocytosis/clearance, and APOE isoform-specific effects on lipidation/interaction with receptors and extracellular matrix — all of which influence perivascular flow and solute removal.

3) Bridge Hypothesis (succinct)
APOE- and receptor-dependent impairment of perivascular/glymphatic and transvascular clearance produces regional retention of CSF-administered gadobutrol at delayed imaging (≈48 h). The degree and topography of gadobutrol enrichment (quantified using FreeSurfer regional segmentation) will correlate with APOE genotype, Aβ/tau burden, and molecular signatures of astrocyte/microglial receptor dysfunction (e.g., AQP4 mislocalization, reduced LRP1), thereby linking Cluster A molecular pathology to Cluster B tracer-imaging phenotypes.

4) Mechanistic steps (how the bridge works)
- APOE4 (or other detrimental variants) causes altered lipidation and receptor interactions → changes in astrocyte and endothelial function.
- Astrocyte AQP4 mislocalization and altered perivascular basal lamina composition impede convective/paravascular flow of CSF into/out of the interstitium.
- Endothelial receptor dysfunction (e.g., reduced LRP1) impairs transcytosis-mediated Aβ efflux across the BBB.
- Net effect: slowed clearance of Aβ/tau and any CSF tracers (gadobutrol) → increased parenchymal tracer retention at delayed time points.
- Regional susceptibility (e.g., medial temporal, parietal cortex) reflects regional differences in vascular architecture, receptor expression, and amyloid/tau deposition — measurable by FreeSurfer-based regional tracer quantification.

5) Falsifiable predictions / experiments
- Human study: intrathecal gadobutrol MRI with baseline and 48-h scans. Use FreeSurfer to generate regional tracer-enrichment maps. Correlate regional tracer retention with:
  - APOE genotype (E4 vs E3/E2)
  - Aβ PET and tau PET burden (regional co-localization expected)
  - CSF biomarkers (Aβ42/40, p-tau)
  - MRI measures of BBB permeability (DCE-MRI) and sleep metrics
Prediction: APOE4 carriers and subjects with higher amyloid/tau burden will have higher delayed parenchymal gadobutrol retention, especially in regions prone to AD pathology.
- Animal models: compare ApoE isoform knock-in mice; manipulate AQP4 expression or polarization; measure kinetics of intrathecal fluorescent tracers and gadobutrol-analog retention and Aβ clearance. Prediction: models with ApoE4 or disrupted AQP4 show delayed tracer clearance and accelerated Aβ accumulation.
- Intervention study: pharmacologically or genetically restore AQP4 polarity or boost LRP1 expression; expect reduced tracer retention and lower interstitial Aβ.
- Imaging validation: co-register tracer maps with amyloid/tau PET and FreeSurfer ROI volumes; test whether tracer retention predicts future amyloid/tau accumulation or neurodegeneration longitudinally.

6) Practical/technical notes and caveats
- Route of administration matters: intrathecal (CSF) gadobutrol imaging probes glymphatic/paravascular dynamics; IV gadolinium mainly probes BBB leakage and is confounded by retention mechanisms.
- Gadobutrol is extracellular and non-specific; retention indicates slowed solute clearance or barrier trapping but not receptor-specific binding.
- Distinguishing BBB leakage (parenchymal entry from blood) from impaired glymphatic clearance (CSF→parenchyma accumulation and slow efflux) requires multimodal protocols (intrathecal vs IV tracers; DCE-MRI; PET).
- Safety/regulatory constraints: intrathecal gadolinium is off-label and requires careful ethics; some gadolinium deposition concerns exist.
- Correlation ≠ causation — mechanistic animal experiments and receptor/transport perturbations are required to prove causality.

7) Immediate next steps to operationalize the bridge
- Design a cross-sectional human pilot: intrathecal gadobutrol with MRI at multiple timepoints including ~48 h; genotype for APOE; perform amyloid/tau PET; quantify regional tracer retention using FreeSurfer segmentations; test correlations.
- Parallel rodent programs: ApoE isoform models + AQP4 manipulations + fluorescent tracer kinetics + histological receptor mapping.
- Develop analysis pipelines: standardized ROI extraction (FreeSurfer), normalize tracer signal to CSF/venous references, model clearance kinetics regionally.

Conclusion
There is a biologically plausible, testable bridge connecting Cluster A (APOE, Aβ, tau, glial/neuronal receptors) and Cluster B (gadobutrol tracer enrichment, 48-h imaging, FreeSurfer quantification): dysfunction of perivascular/glymphatic and receptor-mediated vascular clearance pathways driven by APOE and glial/endothelial receptor changes causes both accumulation of pathological proteins and delayed parenchymal tracer retention measurable with gadobutrol MRI. Testing this hypothesis would create a mechanistic and translational link between molecular Alzheimer’s biology and in vivo tracer-imaging phenotypes.
